The Ledger of the Vellmar Bridge

I.

The bridge at Vellmar was built in 1847 by a company that went bankrupt before the first winter, and for forty years afterwards nobody could say who owned it. The county paid a keeper anyway. The keeper's job was to raise the toll gate, to sweep the deck after storms, and to write in the ledger.

Anna Wrede took the post in 1889, when she was thirty-one and recently widowed. She had kept her husband's accounts at the brickworks for nine years, and the county clerk, who disliked arguing, decided that a woman who could balance a brickworks could certainly balance a bridge.

The ledger she inherited ran back to 1851. Every keeper had written in it. Some had written almost nothing: a name, a date, a number of carts. Others had written too much. The keeper from 1866 to 1871, a man called Petersen, had used the right-hand column to record the weather, his debts, and the names of the dogs that crossed with the drovers.

II.

Anna read the whole ledger in her first month. It took her eleven evenings. She read it because she wanted to know what the work was, and because the house by the bridge was cold and the ledger was the only thing in it that was not cold.

She found the discrepancy on the ninth evening.

Between 1873 and 1881 the tolls collected had risen by a third, which surprised nobody: the railway had come to Hallendorf in 1872 and the goods it brought had to cross the river somehow. But the number of carts recorded had not risen at all. The same figure, between sixty and seventy a week, ran through nine years without moving.

More money, the same number of carts. Either the toll had been raised, or the carts had not been counted.

III.

She asked the county clerk about the toll. He sent back a copy of the schedule: four pfennig for a handcart, twelve for a cart with one horse, twenty for a cart with two, and a shilling for anything on iron wheels. The schedule had not changed since 1858.

So the carts had not been counted. Anna went back to the ledger with a pencil and worked out, week by week, how many carts the money implied. From 1873 the implied number pulled away from the written one, slowly at first, then steadily, until by 1880 the ledger was recording about two carts out of every three.

The keeper in those years was a man named Brandt, who had died in 1884. His entries were neat and unremarkable. He had not stolen the money, because the money was all there, week by week, in the county's own receipts. He had simply written down fewer carts than had crossed.

IV.

It took Anna another two months to understand why, and she understood it because of a sentence in Petersen's column, written twelve years before Brandt arrived: *The bridge shakes under the ore carts and I have written to the county twice.*

She found the two letters in the clerk's office, filed and unanswered. Then she found a third, from Brandt in 1874, asking for an inspection because of a crack in the second pier. It had been answered. The answer said that inspections were ordered when traffic exceeded eighty crossings a week, and that the Vellmar bridge, at sixty-eight, did not qualify.

Brandt had understood the sentence exactly as it was written. If the number rose above eighty, an inspection would be ordered; an inspection would close the bridge; a closed bridge meant no keeper and no house. He had kept the number below eighty for seven years, and the crack had gone on growing in the dark.

V.

Anna wrote her own letter in March 1890. She did not describe the crack, because she knew what happened to letters that described cracks. She wrote out the arithmetic instead: the tolls collected, the schedule of charges, the number of carts those two figures implied, and the number the ledger recorded. She sent a copy to the county and a copy to the newspaper at Hallendorf, and she wrote in the ledger, in the right-hand column, that she had done so.

The inspection came in May. The second pier was shored in June and rebuilt over the following winter, and the bridge stayed open, because a bridge that is being repaired is not a bridge that has fallen.

Anna kept the post until 1911. In her twenty-two years the ledger records no weather, no debts and no dogs. It records carts, and it records them all.
